1.title: The Issues Practice in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: The Issues Practice in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Apply the issues practice: issue management approach, issue register, issue report. Areas of focus of key roles. Issue types, handling steps, change authority, change budget and escalation. Analyze whether an issues approach is effective and fit for purpose considering the principles, the techniques and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (fifty-one percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The issues practice captures, assesses and resolves issues so the project stays in control and the baseline is changed only on purpose. An issue is something that has happened, was not planned and needs management action. The baseline is the approved version of the products and plans. All changes start as issues, but not every issue is a change. It serves manage by exception (decisions at the right level within tolerances), continued business justification (every decision is judged for its effect on the case), focus on products (baselined products are protected), define roles (who decides what) and manage by stages.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The figure shows this: An issue moves from capture through assessment to a decision by the right level, then implementation. Exam tip: Has happened is an issue; might happen is a risk. A request for a new feature is already an issue, because the request has been made.

1.title: The key management products
1.text: The key management products. Issue management approach. How issues and changes are handled: steps, roles, how issues are rated, change control and delegated authority. Part of the initiation documentation. Issue register. A record of all issues, their type, status and the decisions made. Part of the project log. Issue report. A detailed description of one issue, with its impact analysis and a recommendation.

1.title: The key management products, continued
1.text: The key management products. Issue types: a request for change (a proposal to alter a baseline), an off-specification (something that is, or will be, missing from what was agreed) and a problem or concern (anything else needing management action). The book also treats a business opportunity as a possible source of issues. Check the book for the exact list. Exam tip: New wish is a request for change; failing the agreed specification is an off-specification. The type decides the route: a request for change goes through change control.

1.title: Areas of focus of the key roles
1.text: Areas of focus of the key roles. Executive. Decides escalated issues; the business case is protected. Senior user. Judges the user impact of changes and off-specifications. Senior supplier. Judges the impact on the supplier's work and cost. Project manager. Makes sure issues are captured, assessed and managed; escalates when tolerance is threatened. Team manager. Raises issues found in the work packages. Change authority. Approves or rejects changes within the authority delegated by the board. Project assurance. Checks the issue procedure is followed. Project support. Keeps the issue register and records of baselined products. The change budget is a sum the board sets aside to pay for approved changes. The change authority decides within its delegation and the change budget. Check the book's table for exact responsibilities.

1.title: Effective management and techniques
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Capture. Record the issue in the issue register; decide its type; small issues can be dealt with quickly but are still recorded. Assess. Analyze impact on cost, time, quality, scope, benefits, risk and sustainability; consider urgency. Propose. Set out options and a recommendation, in an issue report when it is significant. Decide. The person or group with authority decides, or escalates. Implement. Carry it out; update plans, registers and baselines; tell those affected. The book may word some steps differently; the order and purpose are what matter.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Escalation by tolerance. The project manager decides what can be resolved within the stage tolerance. The change authority decides changes within its delegated limits and the change budget. If a decision would push the stage beyond tolerance, the project manager raises an exception report and the board decides. If project tolerance is threatened, the board goes to the corporate level. Exam tip: Check the tolerance, then the delegation. Inside tolerance and delegation the project manager or change authority decides; outside, escalate. A board decision on every small issue is a red flag, and so is a quiet decision beyond tolerance.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. Every issue is captured and assessed for impact. Issues agreed in corridors or by email and never recorded. Baselined products change only through formal change control. Informal scope creep: a user asks the team and the team just does it. Decided by the right level (project manager, change authority, board). Project manager approves a change beyond tolerance, or the board decides trivial items. Change authority acts within delegated limits and the change budget. Changes approved after the change budget is spent, with no escalation.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Impact on the business case and on benefits considered. Cost of a change judged but its effect on benefits ignored. Registers, plans and baselines updated after the decision. Decision made, but the plan and product register stay unchanged. Lessons recorded from repeat issues. The same off-specification repeats.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring. Small internal project. One person as change authority; a simple register; the same steps. Agile or hybrid delivery. Reordering the backlog inside the baseline and tolerances is routine change control; changes beyond them are formal. Large or multi-party project. Several change authorities; supplier contract variations follow change control. Sustainability or data concerns. Every change is assessed for sustainability and data effects. Exam tip: Agile does not remove change control; it moves the line. Backlog reprioritization within the baseline and tolerances is routine; a change to the baseline or beyond tolerance still goes through formal control.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A harbor pilot asks Wei Chen to add a seasonal permit type to the build. Wei agrees because the work is small and starts it without telling Sam Okafor. Was this appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because it is a proposed change to the baseline and must go through change control. Work package tolerance does not give authority over scope, so the request must be captured and decided at the right level instead of informal scope creep.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A request for change costing six thousand is within the twenty-four thousand change budget and within the authority the board delegated to Tomas Reyes. Who should decide it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Tomas Reyes, change authority. The change authority decides changes within the delegation and change budget, which keeps the board free for exceptions.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A request for change on Project Harbor would cost forty thousand, beyond the twenty-four thousand change budget and the stage tolerance. What should Sam Okafor do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Escalate it to the board with an issue report and a recommendation. The change exceeds both the delegation and the tolerance, so manage by exception requires the board to decide on a recommendation.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Sam Okafor needs a detailed write-up of one off-specification found in testing, with its impact analysis and a recommendation for the board. Which management product is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Issue report. The issue report describes one issue in detail with analysis and recommendation; the register lists all issues and the exception report is for a forecast tolerance breach.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Sam Okafor records a testing defect in the issue register as an off-specification, assesses its impact, and decides to rework it within the stage tolerance. Was this appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because an issue resolved within tolerance may be decided by the project manager once recorded. Within tolerance the project manager decides, provided the issue is captured and assessed, as manage by exception intends.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Wei Chen's agile team reorders backlog items each sprint within the baselined acceptance criteria and stage tolerances. Sam Okafor wonders whether every reorder needs a formal request for change. What should he do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Make reorders within baseline and tolerances routine and send the rest through change control. Tailoring moves where the formal line sits for agile delivery but does not remove change control of the baseline or tolerances.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is an issue? Answer: An event that has happened, was not planned and needs management action. Question two. Name the three issue types. Answer: Request for change, off-specification, and problem or concern. Question three. What is the change budget? Answer: Money the board sets aside to pay for approved changes.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Who decides changes within delegated limits? Answer: The change authority. Question five. What is a baseline? Answer: The approved version of the products and plans used as the reference for control. Question six. When does an issue go to the board? Answer: When resolving it would exceed the project manager's tolerance or the change authority's delegation.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Issue: has happened, unplanned, needs management action. Types: request for change, off-specification, problem or concern. Steps: capture, assess, propose, decide, implement. Change authority: decides changes within delegated limits. Change budget: set aside by the board for approved changes. Issue report: one issue in detail with analysis and recommendation. Escalation: by tolerance: project manager, change authority, board, corporate. Tailoring: agile moves the line; change control of the baseline stays.
